account: Dung 1995 provides the formal backbone for modeling answer-to-answer conflict and belief revision in a question/answer graph. The core definitions—argumentation framework (AF), acceptability, conflict-free sets, admissible sets—all appear on PDF PAGE 6, with the framework's informal introduction straddling pages 5–6. The extension semantics are spread: preferred extensions on page 7, stable extensions and the characteristic function on page 8, and grounded extensions on page 9. Dung explicitly links these semantics to nonmonotonic reasoning and logic programming: stable extensions correspond to stable models, Reiter extensions, and autoepistemic expansions (page 8); Reiter's default logic and logic programming are shown as argumentation (pages 19–24). The source does not discuss belief revision or graph substrates, so mapping AF notions to a Q/A graph is necessarily design inference. From these foundations, we derive that answers map to arguments, conflict edges map to attacks, provenance edges are inert foreign edges, admissible sets define mutually consistent answer sets, preferred extensions define credulous acceptance, the grounded extension defines skeptical acceptance, and belief revision corresponds to mutating the attack relation or argument set and recomputing extensions, with tractability guarded by the incomputability result on page 25.

citations.excerpt: Definition 2. An argumentation framework is a pair AF=(AR,attacks) where AR is a set of arguments, and attacks is a binary relation on AR i.e. attacks ⊆ AR × AR. For two arguments A and B the meaning of attacks(A,B) is that A represents an attack against B.

claims.statement: Dung 1995 defines an argumentation framework as a pair AF=(AR, attacks), where AR is a set of arguments and attacks is a binary relation on AR (attacks ⊆ AR × AR); 'A represents an attack against B' for attacks(A,B).

citations.excerpt: Definition 5. A set S of arguments is said to be conflict-free if there are no arguments A and B in S such that A attacks B. Definition 6. (2) A conflict-free set of arguments S is admissible iff each argument in S is acceptable with respect to S.

claims.statement: Dung 1995 defines a conflict-free set as a set with no internal attacks, and an admissible set as a conflict-free set where each member is acceptable (every attacker is attacked by the set).

citations.excerpt: Definition 7. A preferred extension of an argumentation framework AF is a maximal (with respect to set inclusion) admissible set of AF.

Definition 13. A conflict-free set of arguments S is called a stable extension iff S attacks each argument which does not belong to S. Definition 16. The characteristic function ... F_AF(S) = {A | A is acceptable with respect to S}.
Definition 20. The grounded extension of an argumentation framework AF, denoted by GE_AF, is the least fixed point of F_AF.

claims.statement: Dung 1995 defines three extension semantics: the preferred extension is a maximal admissible set (page 7); the stable extension is a conflict-free set attacking every argument outside it (page 8); the grounded extension is the least fixed point of the characteristic function F_AF (page 9), where F_AF(S) = {A | A is acceptable with respect to S}.

citations.excerpt: This proposition underlines exactly the way the notions of stable models in logic programming, extensions in Reiter's default logic, and stable expansion in Moore's autoepistemic logic are defined.
Theorem 43: Let E be an R-extension of T and E' be a stable extension of AF(T), then arg(E) is a stable extension and flat(E') is an R-extension.
Theorem 49: A Herbrand interpretation M is a stable model of P iff there is a stable extension E of AF(P) ... Theorem 50: The well-founded model of P coincides with the grounded extension of AF(P).

claims.statement: Dung 1995 states that stable models in logic programming, extensions in Reiter's default logic, and stable expansions in Moore's autoepistemic logic are defined in the same way as stable extensions; later sections show Reiter's default logic and logic programming as instances of argumentation, with stable extensions corresponding to R-extensions and stable models.

citations.excerpt: Definition 2. An argumentation framework is a pair AF=(AR,attacks) ... attacks(A,B) is that A represents an attack against B.

claims.statement: Design inference: In the Q/A graph, each answer is an argument; each directed conflict/attack edge from answer A to answer B means accepting A contradicts or defeats B. This maps the answer-to-answer conflict capability of D3 onto Dung's attacks relation.

citations.excerpt: Definition 5. A set S of arguments is said to be conflict-free if there are no arguments A and B in S such that A attacks B.

claims.statement: Design inference: Provenance edges (e.g., answer-addresses-question, answer-derived-from-answer, question-to-question) are separate labeled edge types disjoint from attack edges; because conflict-free sets and acceptability are defined only over the attacks relation, provenance edges do not alter conflict semantics.

citations.excerpt: Definition 7. A preferred extension ... is a maximal admissible set.
Definition 20. The grounded extension ... is the least fixed point of F_AF.

claims.statement: Design inference: Mutually consistent answer sets for a question are admissible sets of the induced argumentation subgraph restricted to answers addressing that question; preferred extensions give credulous acceptance (multiple competing answers coexist), and the grounded extension gives skeptical acceptance (answers accepted regardless of conflict).

citations.excerpt: Definition 13. ... stable extension ... attacks each argument which does not belong to S.
Corollary 12. Every argumentation framework possesses at least one preferred extension.
Theorem 52. ... the stable, well-founded and preferred extension semantics of P are in general incomputable.

counterevidence: The source does not mention belief revision; this is pure design inference.
claims.statement: Design inference: Belief revision is modeled by mutating the attack relation or the set of arguments (adding/retracting answers) and recomputing the relevant extensions; because Dung shows stable extensions need not exist and general extension computation is incomputable, the design must fall back on preferred or grounded acceptance and restrict computation to a finite relevant subgraph.

counterevidence: The source text contains no mention of belief revision, Q/A graphs, or graph substrates; all mappings from AF semantics to the Q/A graph must be treated as design inference, not source claims.

The source explicitly warns that stable extensions may not exist for every framework (e.g., the SMPG example on page 18 and the self-defeating argument example on page 31), so belief revision cannot rely on stable semantics alone.

The source's incomputability result for general logic-programming semantics (page 25) implies that computing extensions over an unbounded answer graph may be undecidable; any design must bound the argument set.
child-4 flags a potential boundary mismatch: the source has no notion of belief revision, so claiming Dung 'defines' belief revision would overstate the evidence and violate D13.
unresolved: The exact syntax and directionality of attack edges (directional vs. bidirectional) is not resolved by Dung's text; the design must choose a convention.
The mapping from natural-language answer conflict to a machine-checkable attack relation is not specified by the source; this is a model-level inference task.
The treatment of weighted or typed conflicts (e.g., specificity vs. contradiction) is not addressed by Dung's binary attack relation.

The exact trigger semantics for when belief revision is performed (e.g., new answer, conflict edge added, explicit user request) is not defined in this node and must come from the parent's runtime specification.
